posts.title: The Career Growth Paradox: You Are Being Promoted Into a Job You Will Be Bad At, On Purpose
posts.excerpt: The skills that get you promoted are almost never the skills the new job needs, and everyone running the promotion already knows it.
posts.content:
*A 2am essay for anyone who just got "great news" from HR*

---

Somewhere right now, someone is opening an email with the subject line "Exciting News About Your Role" and their stomach is dropping like they just failed a bar exam. That is correct. That is the correct emotional response. Because in the modern workplace, being told you are excellent at your job is very often the last step before someone hands you a completely different job that you have never done, gives you zero training for it, and calls the whole thing an opportunity.

This is the career growth paradox, and once you see it you cannot unsee it. The entire system is built to reward you for being good at something by removing you from that something forever.

Let that sit for a second. Then let's ruin your evening properly with data.

## The Premise Nobody Wants To Say Out Loud

Here is the paradox in one sentence: the skills that get you promoted are almost never the skills the next job actually requires, and everybody in charge of promoting you already knows this and does it anyway.

This is not a vibe. This is not a LinkedIn thought leader having a feeling in an airport lounge. This is decades of organizational research, and the punchline is always the same. Companies do not promote people because they will be good at the next job. They promote people because they were good at the last one, which is a completely different metric being used as a proxy for a completely different skill set, the same way you would hire a chef based on how well he grows tomatoes.

Researchers at MIT, the University of Minnesota, and Yale sat down with data from over two hundred firms, more than fifteen hundred employees promoted into management, and something like a hundred and fifty six million individual sales transactions, because apparently someone finally got tired of this being a joke and decided to check. The finding was almost insultingly simple. The better a salesperson was at selling, the more likely they were to get promoted into managing other salespeople, and the more likely their new team's numbers were to quietly tank once they took over.

The skill that got them promoted, closing deals, had almost nothing to do with the skill the new job required, which was coaching other humans to close deals. Nobody bothered to check if those were the same muscle. They are not. They have never been the same muscle. A surgeon does not automatically know how to run a hospital. A brilliant campaign strategist does not automatically know how to govern. And your best engineer does not automatically know how to sit in a room and tell four other engineers why their code is bad without making them cry.

This got a name back in 1969, decades before the research caught up to confirm it. It is called the Peter Principle, and the short version is brutal: in a hierarchy, every employee tends to rise until they reach the level at which they are incompetent, and then they simply stay there, forever, blocking the doorway, running your quarterly planning meeting.

## Chart: What Actually Happens After a Promotion

![](https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/A%20minimalist%20abstract%20line%20chart%20illustration%2C%20two%20hand-drawn%20style%20lines%20on%20a%20soft%20gradient%20background%2C%20one%20line%20rising%20then%20dropping%20sharply%20at%20a%20marker%20point%2C%20another%20line%20flat%20then%20declining%2C%20clean%20flat%20vector%20infographic%20style%2C%20soft%20pastel%20colors%2C%20no%20readable%20text%2C%20no%20words%2C%20no%20letters%2C%20no%20numbers%2C%20no%20labels%2C%20no%20typography?width=1024&height=1024&model=flux&nologo=true&enhance=true&seed=101)

The most quietly devastating part of the whole thing is that this is not really a bug that companies are trying to fix. Some economists argue it is closer to a deliberate strategy. If everyone knew that being excellent at your job guaranteed you would stay in it forever, doing the same thing, nobody would try particularly hard. So companies dangle the promotion as the carrot, fully aware that a meaningful chunk of the people who reach for it will be worse at the next level, because the alternative, a workforce with zero incentive to excel, is somehow considered the bigger risk. You are not a person being developed. You are an incentive structure wearing a lanyard.

## The Loyalty Paradox: Staying Used To Be For Suckers. Now Leaving Is.

For about a decade, the entire career advice industry ran on one instruction, repeated at every brunch, every group chat, every unsolicited uncle at Thanksgiving: never wait for a raise, just leave. Job hopping was the only real lever. Stay at a company more than two years and you were basically volunteering to be underpaid out of a strange sense of nostalgia.

That math has quietly, almost silently, flipped.

In early 2025, workers who switched jobs got a median raise of about 4.8 percent. Workers who stayed put and did absolutely nothing dramatic got 4.6 percent. That is not a premium. That is a rounding error. Two years earlier, in 2023, job hoppers were pulling in 7.7 percent raises against 5.5 percent for the loyalists, a real and meaningful gap. By 2026 that gap had shrunk to numbers so small you would burn more calories updating your resume than the raise was worth.

And here is the part that really should make you angry: for the people at the very top of the income ladder, staying is now winning outright. Top earners who stayed loyal to their employer were pulling in raises approaching double digits, while their peers who jumped ship for a "better opportunity" got a low single digit bump and a new Slack workspace to learn. Meanwhile roughly half of everyone who stayed put, and forty four percent of everyone who left, got no raise at all, or a pay cut, because apparently that is just a coin flip now built into having a job.

## Chart: The Job Hopping Premium, Rest In Peace

![](https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/A%20minimalist%20abstract%20bar%20chart%20illustration%2C%20two%20rows%20of%20bars%20across%20several%20columns%2C%20the%20bars%20becoming%20nearly%20identical%20height%20toward%20the%20right%20side%2C%20muted%20blue%20and%20coral%20color%20palette%2C%20clean%20flat%20vector%20infographic%20style%2C%20small%20subtle%20tombstone%20icon%20in%20the%20corner%2C%20no%20readable%20text%2C%20no%20words%2C%20no%20letters%2C%20no%20numbers%2C%20no%20labels%2C%20no%20typography?width=1024&height=1024&model=flux&nologo=true&enhance=true&seed=101)

So the entire generation that was told loyalty is for suckers grew up, followed the advice, hopped jobs like it was a personality trait, and arrived at the exact moment the data quietly reversed the recommendation without telling anyone. Gen Z switched jobs more than twice as often as Gen X did at the same stage, and it is still paying off for them at the entry level, mostly in competitive blue collar and skilled trade sectors. But the moment you climb high enough to actually be worth real money, the entire strategy inverts and the company that already knows you becomes more valuable than any recruiter's cold DM.

Nobody sent a memo. You were just supposed to know.

## The Middle Management Trap: Congratulations, You Are Now Everyone's Punching Bag

Let's talk about what actually happens once you survive the Peter Principle, dodge the loyalty trap, and land the title anyway. You become a manager. People will now say "wow, look at you" at parties. Your parents will finally understand what you do, sort of. You will also, statistically, become one of the most miserable people in the entire organization, and the data on this is not subtle.

Middle managers now report higher daily stress than the people below them and the executives above them, according to Gallup's most recent global workplace research. Forty five percent of middle managers report burnout, a higher rate than any other job category measured, while only about one in five say they are actually thriving. The average manager is now responsible for roughly twelve direct reports, up fifty percent from just over a decade ago, because every layoff round quietly removes headcount and never removes responsibility.

More than two thirds of managers received no formal training for the job they are now expected to be excellent at. They are, in the actual language researchers use for this, "accidental managers." You were good at the job, so now you manage the job, with no instruction manual, no orientation, and a calendar that is now seventy percent meetings about the meetings you had yesterday.

![](https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/A%20satirical%20illustration%20of%20a%20stressed%20office%20worker%20squeezed%20as%20the%20filling%20inside%20a%20giant%20sandwich%2C%20bread%20on%20top%20and%20bottom%2C%20tiny%20chat%20bubble%20and%20envelope%20icons%20spilling%20out%20the%20sides%20like%20condiments%2C%20cartoon%20editorial%20style%2C%20bright%20and%20slightly%20absurd%2C%20no%20text%2C%20no%20words%2C%20no%20letters%2C%20no%20numbers?width=1024&height=1024&model=flux&nologo=true&enhance=true&seed=101)

## Chart: The Sandwich Nobody Ordered

This is the part of the paradox nobody puts on the recruiting poster. You spend the first ten years of your career trying to escape being told what to do, and the reward at the end of that race is a job where you are responsible for everything and in control of almost nothing. You cannot approve the budget. You cannot approve the headcount. But you can absolutely be blamed when the budget and the headcount do not add up.

## The Specialist's Curse, Or Why Getting Really Good At Your Job Is A Trap

Here is the quietest, cruelest version of the paradox, and it applies whether or not you ever become a manager at all. The deeper you specialize, the more valuable you become at doing one exact thing, and the harder it becomes for anyone to imagine you doing anything else. You built a beautiful, deep, narrow well of expertise, and then you discover the only ladder available goes sideways, out of the well entirely, into general management, where none of that specific expertise matters anymore.

So you have two options, and organizational psychology will happily lay them out for you with a straight face. Option one, stay a brilliant specialist forever, get quietly passed over for leadership roles because "we need you where you are," and watch your title stay flat while your responsibilities creep upward like ivy on a wall nobody is maintaining. Option two, leave the thing you are actually good at to manage other people doing the thing you used to be good at, and slowly watch that skill atrophy while you learn an entirely new, mostly thankless skill from scratch, in public, while everyone watches.

Both options are dressed up as growth. Neither one feels like it, from the inside, at two in the morning, when you are staring at the ceiling wondering why the promotion you worked five years for feels like grief.

## The Paradox Cheat Sheet

![](https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/A%20single%20office%20chair%20on%20a%20mountain%20summit%20made%20of%20stacked%20paperwork%20and%20coffee%20cups%20instead%20of%20rock%2C%20a%20tiny%20exhausted%20person%20sitting%20in%20it%20looking%20at%20a%20glowing%20phone%20with%20a%20small%20notification%20dot%2C%20sunrise%20in%20the%20background%2C%20whimsical%20editorial%20illustration%20style%2C%20warm%20color%20palette%2C%20no%20text%2C%20no%20words%2C%20no%20letters%2C%20no%20numbers?width=1024&height=1024&model=flux&nologo=true&enhance=true&seed=101)

## So What Do You Actually Do With Any Of This

Nothing here is an argument for staying still. Standing still has its own paradox, and it is not a kind one. The point is smaller and meaner than that. The point is that the ladder was never actually a ladder. It was a series of different jobs wearing the same job's clothes, and every single rung requires you to leave behind the exact thing that got you noticed in the first place.

Knowing that will not fix your Tuesday. But it might stop you from lying awake wondering what you did wrong when the answer, honestly, is nothing. You did the job well. That was always going to be the problem.

---

*If this kept you up past 2am, it did its job. Go to bed. The promotion will still be a trap in the morning.*

---

### Sources referenced

Peter Principle research: NBER, Yale School of Management, Journal of Political Economy. Job switching versus staying data: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta Wage Growth Tracker, Bank of America Institute, ADP. Middle management burnout data: Gallup State of the Global Workplace 2025, DDI Global Leadership Forecast, Robert Walters.

posts.title: Anything That Can Go Wrong: The True Story of Murphy's Law
posts.excerpt: A backwards-wired sensor, a daredevil on a rocket sled, and the physics that proves your toast really does hate you.
posts.content:
*Written at 2am, because the only honest time to write about everything going wrong is while something is.*

You know the moment. It is 2am. You have one small job left before bed. Save the file. Send the text. Carry the plate to the sink. And that is exactly when the laptop freezes, the message lands in the wrong chat, and the toast leaves your hand in slow motion and comes down, without fail, butter-side first, on the one rug you actually care about.

We have a name for that feeling. We say it under our breath like a curse and a prayer at the same time. Murphy's Law. Anything that can go wrong will go wrong.

Here is the part almost nobody knows. Murphy's Law was not handed down by some gloomy philosopher. It was born on a military base in the California desert, out of a near-fatal crash test, a backwards-wired sensor, and one very irritated engineer who never wanted his name anywhere near it. And the strangest twist of all is that the toast thing is real. A physicist proved it, won a prize for it, and the universe has been quietly smug about it ever since.

This is the story of how a complaint became a law.

## The desert, the sled, and the man who was not amused

In 1949, the United States Air Force was chewing on a brutal question. How much force can a human body survive before it comes apart? Jets were getting faster. Pilots were ejecting at speeds that had never existed before. Somebody had to find the limit, and the only honest way to find it was to build a machine that could nearly kill a volunteer and then stop just short.

That machine was a rocket sled nicknamed the Gee Whiz. It ran down a half-mile track at Edwards Air Force Base, hit speeds well past 200 miles per hour, then slammed to a halt in under a second. The man strapped to it was Colonel John Paul Stapp, a flight surgeon with a death wish dressed up as scientific curiosity. On one run he reached 632 miles per hour and took 46.2 G, which made him, for a while, the fastest human being on the ground. He finished test runs with broken bones, burst blood vessels, and detached retinas, and then he climbed back on.

Into this project walked Captain Edward A. Murphy Jr., an engineer from Wright Field. Murphy had designed a set of sensors, strain gauges, meant to measure the exact forces hitting Stapp's body during a run. On the day that matters, his assistant wired the four gauges into the harness, the sled fired, and the readout came back as a flat, useless zero. Every single sensor had been installed backwards.

That is the moment. Standing there, looking at a failed test and a wasted run on a one-of-a-kind machine, Murphy grumbled something close to the line that would outlive everyone in the room.

> If there is any way to do it wrong, he will find it.

It was a jab at a technician. It was not meant to be profound. Murphy got in his car, drove back home to Ohio, and as far as he knew, that was the end of it.

![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/5593ff54-1d1f-425a-9017-5d33bd664122/7bce8bcb-aa31-44ef-be1d-f44943911745/ChatGPT_Image_Jun_14_2026_04_23_02_PM.png)

## How a grumble escaped the lab

Here is where it gets interesting. Stapp, the man on the sled, had a gift for a quote. At a later press conference, a reporter asked how nobody on such a dangerous project had been seriously hurt. Stapp credited the team's safety record to something he called Murphy's Law, and explained it roughly as the idea that anything that can go wrong, will. The reporters loved it. They wrote it down.

From there it spread the way good ideas spread, which is to say it stopped belonging to anyone. It turned up in aerospace trade articles in the 1950s. A character explained it in a 1958 stage play. Engineers adopted it as a design philosophy, because in their world a single thing going wrong could drop an aircraft out of the sky. By the time Arthur Bloch published his Murphy's Law books in the late 1970s, the phrase had hardened into folk wisdom, printed on mugs and office posters and bathroom walls all over the world.

![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/5593ff54-1d1f-425a-9017-5d33bd664122/3a79d711-a3ed-47ae-9462-1adbc6fee41b/03_timeline.png)

The real Edward Murphy, by most accounts, hated it. He felt the popular version twisted his meaning. He had not been making a gloomy prophecy about an unfair universe. He had been making a flat engineering point. If a part can be installed two ways, and one of them is wrong, then sooner or later somebody will install it the wrong way, so you had better design it so the wrong way is impossible.

That is not pessimism. That is defensive design, and it is the reason your phone charger, your USB-C cable, and the critical connectors on an airplane are built so they physically cannot go in backwards. Murphy was not warning you that life is cruel. He was telling you to idiot-proof the harness.

## So is it real, or are we just whining?

This is the question everyone actually wants answered. Does the universe really lean toward disaster, or do we just remember the bad days louder than the good ones?

For decades it was a bar argument with no referee. Then, in 1995, a British physicist named Robert Matthews decided to settle at least one piece of it. The toast.

The buttered-toast belief is the purest, most universal example of Murphy's Law. Knock a slice off the table and it seems to land butter-side down with a frequency that feels personal. The popular explanation was that the butter weighs one side down. Matthews showed that this is nonsense. The butter is far too light to matter. The real culprit is geometry, gravity, and the boringly average height of your dining table.

Here is what actually happens. When toast slides off the edge of a table, it does not fall flat. It tips, and as it tips it begins to rotate. The only question is how far it can spin before it hits the floor. And it turns out that a normal table, around 75 centimeters tall, gives the slice just enough falling time to complete roughly half a rotation. Half a rotation means the side that started up, the buttered side, ends up down.

![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/5593ff54-1d1f-425a-9017-5d33bd664122/e505496f-a238-4865-8d1a-d9b26b6fffd8/01_toast_rotation.png)

The grim comedy is in the math. To give the toast enough air time for a full rotation, so it lands butter-side up again, your table would need to be about three meters tall. We do not build three-meter tables, and we cannot, because table height is tied to human height, and human height is capped by the strength of the chemical bonds holding your bones together. Matthews followed that chain all the way down to the fundamental constants of physics and concluded, with a completely straight face, that toast lands butter-side down because of the structure of the universe itself. The work won him an Ig Nobel Prize in 1996, the award for research that makes you laugh and then makes you think.

But a theory is just a theory until somebody drops the bread. So in 2001, Matthews helped run a mass experiment with around a thousand British schoolchildren. They dropped toast 9,821 times and recorded which way it landed.

![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/5593ff54-1d1f-425a-9017-5d33bd664122/6579c9a4-25a7-48ae-a85b-b83cd894e930/02_toast_experiment.png)

The toast landed butter-side down 62 percent of the time. Not 50. Not random. The carpet really is winning. For this one specific, buttery corner of human experience, Murphy's Law is not a feeling. It is a measurable, repeatable fact.

## Why your brain is rigged to believe the rest of it

The toast is real. Most of the rest of Murphy's Law, though, lives inside your head, and your head is a deeply unreliable narrator.

Three quirks of human psychology do almost all the work.

The first is negativity bias. We are built to remember threats more vividly than comforts, because the ancestors who shrugged off danger tended not to become ancestors. A smooth commute evaporates by lunchtime. The one morning the car would not start replays for a week. Over a lifetime, that lopsided recording makes disaster feel far more common than it is.

The second is confirmation bias. The moment you learn the phrase Murphy's Law, you start hunting for it. Every dropped slice, every slow checkout, every rained-out picnic becomes evidence. Aha, Murphy again. The hits get filed. The misses get quietly deleted.

The third is selection bias, and the supermarket queue is the perfect example. You feel like you always pick the slowest line. But think it through. There are lines on both sides of you. When yours is the fastest, you sail through and never give it a thought. When yours is the slowest, you stand there stewing, watching everyone else glide past, burning the memory in. You are not cursed. You are simply present for your own delays and absent for your own wins.

> **You are not unlucky. You are just present for every delay you have, and absent for every win.**

![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/5593ff54-1d1f-425a-9017-5d33bd664122/0bc975ba-759b-4cc9-a2a2-f3e702ff916f/ChatGPT_Image_Jun_14_2026_04_23_06_PM.png)

Stack these three together and you get a brain that keeps a meticulous file of every time things went wrong and shreds the receipts for every time things went right. Add the law of truly large numbers, which says that across billions of tiny daily events, some unlikely disasters are basically guaranteed to land on someone, and you have everything you need to believe the universe holds a personal grudge. It does not. It is just enormous, and you are paying selective attention.

## The hall of fame of going wrong

Part of why Murphy's Law went viral, decades before viral meant anything, is that people could not stop adding to it. Engineers, programmers, and tired office workers wrote their own corollaries, each one a little darker and funnier than the last. A few of the best:

And then there is the joke engineering students have been telling for fifty years, the one that accidentally breaks physics. Cats always land on their feet. Toast always lands butter-side down. So strap a buttered slice to a cat's back, butter-side up, drop the cat, and the two laws cancel out. The cat cannot land, and the toast cannot land, so the whole rig hovers a foot above the ground, spinning forever. It is complete nonsense. It is also the most honest thing ever said about Murphy's Law, because it captures the real suspicion underneath all of this. That the universe is not merely difficult, but actively, creatively committed to the bit.

> **A cat always lands on its feet. Toast always lands butter-side down. Strap them together and the universe simply refuses to choose.**

## How to actually use Murphy's Law

Here is the reframe that turns the whole thing from exhausting into useful.

Edward Murphy was right, but not in the way the posters claim. He was not telling you to expect misery. He was telling you to assume that anything which can fail eventually will, and to build your life so that the failure does not matter. That is not despair. That is the most practical advice an engineer ever gave.

So back up the file before you are tired, not after. Build the system so the cable cannot go in backwards. Leave for the airport assuming one thing will go wrong, and let the calm of having planned for it be your reward when it does. Murphy's Law stops being a punishment the second you treat it as a checklist.

The toast will still land butter-side down. That part is physics, and physics does not negotiate. But almost everything else, the blown deadline, the lost work, the disaster with impeccably bad timing, is mostly a failure of preparation wearing the costume of bad luck.

The universe is not out to get you. It is just running the numbers, every second, on everything that could possibly go wrong. Murphy's one real lesson was to run them first

![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/5593ff54-1d1f-425a-9017-5d33bd664122/6cb6380a-2600-426f-8685-24e483e5ba34/ChatGPT_Image_Jun_14_2026_04_23_33_PM.png)

posts.title: Why Your Requirements Keep Changing (It Is Not Your Work. It Is the Clock.)
posts.excerpt: You delivered in 2 days and got one change. You delivered in 5 days and got a committee. Same work. Same person. Different amount of time for people to have opinions.
posts.content:
![A beautiful chaos of sticky notes on a whiteboard representing planning gone wrong](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1531403009284-440f080d1e12?w=1400&q=80)

Picture this.

You finish a task in two days. You send it. Your manager looks at it for thirty seconds and says "looks good, just change the button color."

Now picture the same task. You take five days. You send the exact same work. Suddenly there are three new stakeholders on the review call. Someone questions the entire approach. A business person you have never met in your life has "concerns." A designer who was not part of the brief has feelings about the spacing. And the button color is now the least of your problems.

The work is identical. You are the same person. The output did not change.

But five days somehow created seventeen new opinions.

This is not a you problem. This is not even a manager problem. This is Parkinson's Law showing up to your standup uninvited and eating all the snacks.

---

## First, What Is Parkinson's Law

In 1955, a British historian named C. Northcote Parkinson wrote a now-famous essay. His opening line was this:

> "Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion."

He was writing about bureaucracy and being funny about it. But seventy years later, every person who has ever worked in a team, a startup, a corporation, or a group project in college knows he was also being terrifyingly accurate.

When you give people five days to review something, they will use five days to review it. They will think of new things. They will forward it to other people. Those other people will think of new things. By day four, someone who has never attended a single planning meeting will have three strong opinions about your work.

This is not malicious. This is just what human brains do when given idle time and something to look at.

![People in a meeting with too many stakeholders and too many opinions](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1552664730-d307ca884978?w=1400&q=80)

---

## The Numbers That Should Make Everyone Uncomfortable

This is where it stops being a funny observation and starts being a documented business disaster.

> **$2 trillion** is lost globally every year due to failed or reworked projects. Not million. Trillion. With a T.

> Source: Project Management Institute, 2023

> **40 to 50 percent** of total project time is spent on rework on average. Not building. Not improving. Redoing things that were already done once.

> Source: Keil et al., IEEE Software

> **70 percent of projects** that fail cite poor or changing requirements as the primary reason for failure.

> Source: Standish Group CHAOS Report

> **80 percent of rework** is caused by missing or misunderstood requirements at the start. Not bad execution. Not lazy work. Missing clarity before the work even began.

> Source: American Society for Quality

Let that last one sit for a second. Four out of five revision cycles happen because the brief was incomplete at the start. Not because the work was poor. Not because the team was slow.

The problem walked in on day one and nobody noticed.

---

## The Five Types of People Who Will Change Your Work (A Love Letter)

![Different personalities in every workplace project review](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1560250097-0b93528c311a?w=1400&q=80)

After watching requirements evolve in real time across enough projects, you start to recognize the cast of characters. They appear in every company, every industry, every Slack workspace.

**The Shower Thinker** enters on day three with "I was thinking about this and I feel like we need to rethink the whole approach." Genuinely smart person. Genuinely terrible for project timelines. Means well every single time.

**The Forwarded Email** was never in the original brief. They received a screenshot from someone else and now have seven questions about decisions that were finalized six weeks ago. Nobody knows how they got into the review call.

**The Business Concern** shows up only when the work is almost done. Has never attended a planning session. Has very strong feelings about the font choice and the overall vibe.

**The Scope Creeper** says "can we just add one small thing" eleven times across three different meetings. Each thing is not small. They are always very enthusiastic about it.

**The Silent Approver** said nothing during three full review rounds. Gave a thumbs up at the end. Then sent a message at 11pm asking why the previous version was better and whether we could go back.

You have worked with all five of these people. You have probably been one of them at some point. No judgment at all.

---

## So Is It a Planning Problem or a People Problem

Source: Project Management Institute, 2022 Pulse of the Profession

Here is the honest answer that nobody wants to say out loud.

It is almost always a planning problem that looks and feels like a people problem.

When requirements are vague at the start, every single person involved fills in the gaps with their own assumptions. When the actual finished work arrives, all those different assumptions collide at once. The result looks like someone changing their mind. But really, they never had a clearly defined mind to begin with. Nobody did.

The five-day delivery window does not create more changes. It just creates more time for assumptions to turn into opinions.

![Clear structured planning session with whiteboard and alignment](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1454165804606-c3d57bc86b40?w=1400&q=80)

---

## The Positive Side That Nobody Talks About

Here is something worth saying clearly before this turns into a rant with a sad ending.

Not all feedback is scope creep. Not all revision is chaos. Some of the best work in history got better because someone pushed back on it.

The difference between painful rework and healthy iteration is one thing: clarity at the beginning.

> Teams that invest 30 percent more time in requirements definition upfront reduce total project time by 40 percent.

> Source: Software Engineering Institute, Carnegie Mellon University

> Projects with clearly documented and agreed acceptance criteria are 3x more likely to be delivered on time and within budget.

> Source: PMI Pulse of the Profession, 2022

> Teams using agile with clear sprint goals report 60 percent less unplanned rework compared to teams without defined goals.

> Source: McKinsey Digital, 2021

The goal is not to eliminate feedback. Feedback is how good work becomes great work. The goal is to separate genuine improvement from decisions that should have been made before the work ever started.

One is collaboration. The other is just delay wearing a productive costume.

---

## What Good Actually Looks Like

The best project kickoffs in the world answer three questions before a single line of work begins.

**What does done look like?** Not in a vague feel-good way. Specifically. With examples. With something you can point at and say yes or no to.

**Who has the final say?** One person. Not a committee. Not a thread. Not whoever replies fastest. One human with a name and the authority to close the conversation.

**What is out of scope?** This one is uncomfortable and most people skip it. But knowing what you are not building is as valuable as knowing what you are building. Sometimes more.

When these three questions have real answers written down somewhere that everyone has actually read, the two-day vs five-day problem mostly disappears. Because by the time the work lands, everyone already agreed on what they were looking at.

No surprises. No shower thoughts on day four. No Forwarded Email with questions from 2024.

---

## The Real Takeaway

Rework is expensive. Changing requirements mid-flight is expensive. But the people asking for changes are usually not villains. They are just humans operating in a system that never gave them a clear picture at the start.

The fix is boring and unglamorous. It is a better thirty-minute conversation at the beginning. It is writing down what done looks like before anyone starts. It is one brave person in every kickoff meeting willing to ask "before we move, what does approved actually mean here?"

That person is slightly annoying in the moment.

They are also the reason the project ships on time, everyone goes home at a reasonable hour, and the button color gets decided exactly once.

Be that person.

---

*Written at 2 AM because the irony of writing about wasted time while not sleeping felt about right.*
